name: Flavors (JW Marriott Seoul)
summary: Five-star international buffet two stops from home, loved for live seafood stations and a famously strong dessert room.
description: Flavors is the all-day buffet on the 2nd floor of the JW Marriott at Express Bus Terminal — two stops from Nambu Bus Terminal on Line 3 and linked to Shinsegae Gangnam. Stations cover sushi and sashimi, snow crab, carved roasts, Peking duck, noodle soups, Korean dishes and a large dessert section. Naver reviewers single out the seafood quality and desserts, while some regulars feel the grilled meats and menu line-up need refreshing. It is an easy, weather-proof celebration meal for five with valet parking and a hotel-level service team.
highlights: Snow crab and live seafood station
Dessert room (reviewers rank it among Seoul’s best)
tips: Closest luxury buffet to home: Line 3 two stops to Express Bus Terminal, Exit 3, then 2 minutes on foot.
Weekday lunch (₩179,000) is ₩30,000 cheaper than dinner/weekend (₩209,000); Chuseok days are billed at holiday rates.
Reserve by phone or Naver booking and ask for a window-side table for five.
Pair with Shinsegae Gangnam department store next door.

reviews.text: Guests praise the seafood variety — prawns, crab legs and a live seafood station cooked to order — and warm, personal service.
A regular calls the seafood outstanding and the crab, pho and pasta delicious, but found the pre-grilled sirloin dry.
A frequent hotel-buffet diner says food and service are reliably good, though the menu has barely changed in years.

name: The Terrace Kitchen (Grand Hyatt Seoul)
nameKo: 그랜드 하얏트 서울 더 테라스 키친
summary: Renovated Grand Hyatt buffet on Namsan’s slope with floor-to-ceiling views over Seoul and cooked-to-order stations.
description: The Grand Hyatt’s all-day restaurant reopened as The Terrace Kitchen after a renovation, keeping its trademark wall of glass looking over Itaewon, the Han River and southern Seoul. Tables are now spaced wider so most seats get the view, and many dishes are cooked to order at live stations, including a seafood atelier. Naver diners describe menu cards beside each dish and a more course-like feel than a typical buffet. It sits halfway up Namsan, so plan on a taxi rather than the steep walk from Hangangjin Station.
tips: Open through Chuseok with holiday hours 10:00–20:00 on 24–26 Sep (Naver listing).
Take a taxi (≈25–30 min from home) — the walk from Hangangjin Station is 20 minutes uphill.
A Naver reviewer notes vouchers are often cheapest on Naver booking.
Request a window table when booking for a group of five.

reviews.text: Under its former name The Terrace, reviewers called it the nicest-view buffet in Seoul, with an enormous dessert spread and efficient service.
A family of seven celebrating a grandmother’s birthday liked that renovated seating is spaced out so even non-window tables enjoy the view.
A repeat guest says staff explain each dish, and cooked-to-order plates arrive hot — “like a course meal inside a buffet.”

name: The Market Kitchen (Four Seasons Seoul)
nameKo: 포시즌스 호텔 서울 더 마켓 키친
summary: Four Seasons’ market-hall buffet by Gwanghwamun: king crab, lobster, live grills and a sleek marble-and-wood room.
description: Styled like a European market hall, The Market Kitchen sits on the lower level of the Four Seasons at Gwanghwamun, two minutes from the station. Chefs cook à la minute at live stations — grills, carving, seafood, sushi and a crêpe show — with king crab and lobster the big draws on Naver. Reviewers note the hotel preserves Joseon-era remains uncovered during construction, which makes the walk in unusually interesting. It is a comfortable pick before or after Gyeongbokgung and the palaces.
highlights: Crêpe show at the dessert station
tips: Express Lunch (₩109,000) is the cheapest way in; festive-season pricing (₩185,000–219,000) may apply over Chuseok.
Pair with Gyeongbokgung (closed Tuesdays) — 10 minutes on foot.
Book a family table on Naver or by phone; weekends fill quickly.

reviews.text: Travellers describe an international bazaar of dishes prepared à la minute at live cooking stations, with standout seafood and desserts.
A birthday diner was thrilled to have unlimited king crab and lobster, plus the crêpe show — only regret was a small appetite.
A family noticed noticeably warmer, more attentive table service and a revamped grill section on a return visit.

name: Constans (Josun Palace)
summary: Josun Palace’s 24th-floor buffet in Gangnam: art-deco room, city views and dishes cooked on the spot.
description: Constans occupies the 24th floor of Josun Palace, the Luxury Collection hotel above Gangnam Finance Center on Teheran-ro. Gold-lit ceilings, red chairs and patterned marble make it one of the most design-forward buffet rooms in Seoul, and window tables look over Gangnam. Most dishes are cooked to order, from udon and xiaolongbao to grilled short-rib patties and shakshuka. Naver regulars rate the view, fruit and service highly.
tips: Request a window table when booking — Naver reviewers who did say the daytime view is superb.
Weekday lunch (₩175,000) is the best value; weekend lunch/dinner is ₩205,000.
Yeoksam Station Exit 8, 6 minutes; about 20 minutes from home by taxi or Line 2.

reviews.text: Guests describe Constans as a 24th-floor buffet whose view is its biggest advantage, with most dishes cooked on the spot.
A birthday diner who booked ahead got a window seat — “the view is great, different from at night” — and loved the sweet fruit.
A reviewer praises the 24th-floor view over Yeoksam and the attentive managers and chefs.

name: The Parkview (The Shilla Seoul)
summary: The Shilla’s benchmark buffet: snow crab, toro, Peking duck and garden views beside Namsan’s wooded slope.
description: The Parkview is the ground-floor buffet of The Shilla, long regarded by Seoul residents as the city’s benchmark hotel buffet. Windows face the hotel gardens and Namsan’s trees, and the spread spans Korean, Japanese, Chinese, Vietnamese and Italian stations. TripAdvisor reviewers highlight snow crab, toro and Peking duck; Naver diners mention sparkling wine, warm soups and staff heating crab at the table. Weekends are busy, so booking is essential.
highlights: Lamb chops and tenderloin from the grill
tips: Book well ahead for weekends; Chuseok days are priced as holidays (lunch ₩204,000, dinner ₩208,000).
Children’s prices are about half of adult prices.
Valet parking can be slow at peak times — a Naver reviewer waited 40 minutes; take a taxi instead.
Combine with a stroll on the Namsan walking trail or the Shilla sculpture garden.

reviews.text: Reviewers call it a buffet extravaganza — snow crab, toro and Peking duck — and say food and service impress every visit.
Diners loved the tenderloin and xiaolongbao, fresh sashimi, and staff warming the snow crab brought to the table.
Food and service were good, but retrieving the valet-parked car took over 40 minutes.

name: Yu Yuan (Four Seasons Seoul)
summary: Michelin-starred Cantonese room at the Four Seasons: carved Peking duck, dim sum lunches and 1920s-Shanghai glamour.
description: Yu Yuan on the Four Seasons’ 11th floor channels 1920s Shanghai with teal walls, brass screens and lamp-lit tables. The Michelin-starred kitchen is Cantonese at heart: Peking duck carved tableside, barbecued char siu, double-boiled soups and a strong dim sum lunch. Naver reviewers praise balanced seasoning and staff who greet every guest; many choose it for anniversaries and parents’ milestones. Private rooms make it easy for a family of five.
tips: Lunch Delights course (₩140,000) is the gentlest entry; dinner courses run ₩280,000–320,000.
Order the Peking duck in advance when booking.
Ask for a private room for five — ideal for parents.

reviews.text: Reviewers recommend the Peking duck and popular lunchtime dim sum, calling it a good place for family gatherings and special events.
An anniversary diner says it was their most memorable restaurant in a long time — proper Cantonese cooking and Peking duck.
A guest liked the warm greetings from every staff member, the clean luxurious room and perfectly judged seasoning.

name: Palsun (The Shilla Seoul)
summary: The Shilla’s storied Cantonese room: Buddha-jumps-over-the-wall, Peking duck and private rooms made for parents’ milestones.
description: Palsun has been The Shilla’s flagship Chinese restaurant for decades, serving refined Cantonese banquet cooking in a calm, backlit room with seven small-to-medium private rooms and two large ones. Signatures include Buddha-jumps-over-the-wall, braised abalone and sea cucumber, and Peking duck. Naver reviewers describe 70th-birthday family lunches, with staff helping hang banners and taking the family photo. It is expensive but polished and quiet.
tips: Private rooms are hard to get — reserve weeks ahead and mention a party of five.
Lunch courses (₩200,000–250,000) cost less than dinner (₩230,000–500,000).
Staff will help with celebration touches (banners, family photos) if asked.

reviews.text: Reviewers praise first-class service, premium seafood such as Buddha-jumps-over-the-wall, and one of Seoul’s best Peking ducks.
A family marking a parent’s 70th birthday thanks staff for helping set up a banner, explaining every dish and taking a family photo.
The renewed Buddha-jumps-over-the-wall tastes even better, and the fried pork ribs are light and clean.

name: Pierre Gagnaire à Séoul
summary: Pierre Gagnaire’s French restaurant on Lotte Hotel’s 35th floor: Murano chandeliers, gold trim and a sweep over Seoul.
description: Opened in 2008 atop the Lotte Hotel’s New Wing, this is the three-Michelin-star Parisian chef’s Seoul outpost, listed in the current Michelin Guide Seoul selection. The dining room is classic French luxury — Murano chandeliers, gold trim, orange velvet chairs — with windows over downtown and Namsan. Courses are multi-part and playful in Gagnaire’s style, using mostly local ingredients. TripAdvisor opinions are mixed on value, but Naver diners consistently praise the view, service and set-piece dishes.
tips: Lunch Déjeuner (₩180,000) gives the view at the lowest price; dinner courses are ₩280,000–320,000.
Ask for a window table or the private room for five when reserving.
Euljiro 1-ga Station Exit 8 connects almost directly to the hotel.

reviews.text: Reviewers admire artfully presented food and one of the best views in Seoul, though some feel prices outrun the experience.
“Truly the best” — a diner who upgraded to the steak main says every plate showed top-level care, especially a wheat risotto.
A guest loved the view, quiet atmosphere and very kind staff, and would return for the course.

name: STAY by Yannick Alléno (Signiel Seoul)
summary: Yannick Alléno’s modern French restaurant on Lotte World Tower’s 81st floor — sky-high Han River views with every course.
description: STAY sits on the 81st floor of Lotte World Tower inside the Signiel hotel, with a black-and-white checkerboard floor, gold pendant lights and full-height windows over the Han River and Jamsil. The menu, designed by multi-Michelin-starred chef Yannick Alléno, runs from accessible lunch sets to lavish tasting menus. It is listed in the current Michelin Guide Seoul selection. Naver diners rank the view first, then food and service; a few feel value is only average.
tips: Window seats cost an extra ₩30,000 on Fri–Sun lunches per a Naver reviewer — worth it on a clear day.
STAY Fun (₩135,000) is the entry course; pair with Seoul Sky or Lotte World Mall.
Jamsil Station Exit 2 connects directly to the tower.

reviews.text: A reviewer calls STAY “truly the best restaurant we dined at in Seoul,” praising the chef’s team for memorable dishes.
On the 81st floor the Han River view justified the window-seat supplement; courses from amuse-bouche to dessert were well paced.
Food was tasty and staff kind enough to take a group photo, but value for money felt slightly lacking.

name: Oreno Ramen (Main)
summary: Michelin Bib Gourmand ramen in Hapjeong: creamy chicken paitan broth, blended to a froth, for about ₩13,000.
description: Oreno Ramen’s original Hapjeong shop has been a Michelin Bib Gourmand every year since 2019, according to Naver diners, and it is the city’s best-known tori paitan (chicken-bone) ramen. The broth is blitzed until frothy and served with chicken chashu, wood-ear mushrooms and a soft egg; the spicy kara paitan is the local favourite. Ordering is by kiosk and seating is mostly a counter plus small tables. Expect a line at peak meal times, but turnover is quick.
tips: Open through Chuseok with regular 11:00–22:00 hours on 24–26 Sep (Naver listing) — rare for a Hongdae-area favourite.
No break time: go around 14:30–16:30 on a weekday to skip the queue, as Naver diners recommend.
Choose coriander or kimchi at the kiosk; seats are mostly counter, so a group of five may be split.

reviews.text: A diner notes it has been a Michelin Bib Gourmand for eight straight years since 2019, explaining the long queues outside.
A regular says the spicy kara paitan still makes them exclaim at the first sip — a silky, blender-foamed white broth.
Travel guides describe a clean, less greasy chicken broth, with refills available on noodles, rice and broth.

name: Kyodaiya
summary: Bib Gourmand Sanuki udon cut to order by two brothers in Hapjeong — bouncy noodles and famously crisp tempura.
description: Kyodaiya (“brothers’ shop”) is run by two chef brothers who roll and cut Sanuki-style udon for every order, so the noodles keep their spring and gloss. The kake udon uses a light iriko (dried sardine) broth, while the chilled bukkake and zaru udon show off the texture best. Naver diners rave about the tempura as much as the noodles. The Michelin Guide lists it as a Bib Gourmand.
highlights: Udon set meals with rice and pickles
tips: Closed 24–27 Sep for Chuseok and every Monday — go Wed 23, Tue 29 or Wed 30 (Naver listing).
Take a numbered ticket and pre-order while waiting; arriving before 11:30 usually means a short wait.
Set meals (₩15,500–17,500) add rice, tempura and sides — enough for a hungry parent.

reviews.text: The Michelin Guide lists Kyodaiya as a Bib Gourmand for its freshly cut Sanuki-style udon.
A weekday lunch diner found the noodles as chewy as rice cakes and called the tempura “insane — the best of my life.”
Arriving around 11 a.m. meant a 10-minute wait; you take a ticket and order ahead, and the noodles are superb.

name: Jeongdon Gangnam
summary: Thick, juicy premium tonkatsu by Sinnonhyeon — a Seoul tonkatsu institution with a spacious, clean Gangnam branch.
description: Jeongdon made its name with thick-cut rosy tenderloin and loin katsu fried in a light, crackling crust, and the Gangnam branch is its roomiest location. Sets pair katsu with rice, miso and pickles, and there are black-tiger prawn katsu and zaru soba or udon tempura sets. Naver diners mention an instruction card explaining how to eat each cut, and several bring their parents. The room is bright and tidy, with enough tables for a group of five.
tips: Closed 24–25 Sep for Chuseok (Naver notice); reopens Sat 26.
Tenderloin sells out by evening — go at 11:30 opening or right after the 17:00 break.
3 minutes from Sinnonhyeon Station Exit 4 (Line 9 / Sinbundang); about 15 minutes from home by taxi.

The meat is very thick yet tender, and the crust stays crisp to the last bite; sauces don’t overpower the pork.
An English-language review describes juicy, crispy cutlets and generous portions, three minutes from Sinnonhyeon Station.

name: Menya Sandaime (Hongdae)
summary: Hongdae ramen-ya that feels like a Tokyo backstreet: rich tonkotsu, tsukemen and crisp-winged gyoza from ₩10,000.
description: Menya Sandaime has been a Hongdae ramen reference for over a decade, with a noren-hung wooden front and a small, Japanese-feeling room. The classic is a creamy tonkotsu with chashu and wood-ear mushroom, alongside spicy karakuchi, black-garlic kuro ramen, tsukemen and mazesoba. Naver diners say it feels like being on a trip to Japan; TripAdvisor reviewers call it the real deal. It is small and busy, so it suits a quick lunch rather than a long family meal.
tips: Open daily 11:30–22:00 with no break; closes early if broth sells out.
Small room — a group of five may be split; go before 12:00 or after 14:00.
Add the ₩4,000 chashu rice bowl for a bigger meal.

reviews.text: Reviewers say the ramen is the real deal and the gyoza great, though the small shop often has people waiting outside.
The atmosphere and Japanese staff made a diner feel like they were travelling in Japan — delicious and well priced.
A diner who dislikes heavy pork broths loved the subtle katsuobushi note in the ramen.

name: Damtaek
summary: Bib Gourmand shio ramen near Hapjeong: clear, delicate chicken-seafood broth with a bright yuzu version.
description: Damtaek is a small, minimalist ramen shop on a Seogyo-dong side street that the Michelin Guide lists as a Bib Gourmand. Its speciality is shio (salt) ramen — a clear, gently sweet broth with tender chashu — plus yuzu shio, wasabi and prawn versions and a neungi-mushroom mazemen. Naver diners praise the chewy noodles and free extra rice or noodles. It is far less known to foreign visitors than Oreno, a 10-minute walk away.
tips: Closed on Chuseok day (25 Sep) and every Sunday; open 24 and 26 Sep (Naver).
Last order 20:00 and break 15:00–17:00.
Ask for a free top-up of noodles or rice.

reviews.text: Listed by the Michelin Guide Seoul as a Bib Gourmand for its shio ramen.

summary: Charcoal yakitori omakase in Yeonnam from chef Kim Byoung-mook, the “yakitori king” of Netflix’s Culinary Class Wars.
description: Chef Kim Byoung-mook grills free-range chicken over binchotan and straw along a long open counter, working through thigh, heart, skin and tsukune with a poached egg. The Michelin Guide Seoul lists the restaurant, and his run on Netflix’s Culinary Class Wars made seats harder to get. Naver diners call the omakase juicy and good value for the quality, though one found a recent visit over-salted. There is also a newer Sinsa branch closer to home.
tips: Dinner only, 17:00–23:00 (last order 22:00); book on CatchTable.
One drink per person (or one bottle per table) is required; corkage ₩30,000 per wine/sake bottle.
Counter seating — ask for five seats together, or try the Sinsa branch.

reviews.text: DanielFoodDiary calls chef Kim the “yakitori king,” grilling fresh chicken over charcoal and straw at a long open counter.
An omakase diner says it was the juiciest yakitori they have ever had and great value for a course.
A fan of the Sinsa branch found the main shop’s skewers too salty and overcooked on one visit.
